PMGT1711 Week 09

PMGT1711 Week 9 - Temporal Complexity and Mapping Project Complexity

Temporal Complexity

Temporal complexity arises when a project encounters significant environmental changes outside its direct influence or control. The team may expect change without knowing its form or timing. Examples include mergers, leadership changes, organisational restructuring, changes of government and new legislation.

A long duration increases exposure to such changes. Large infrastructure, aerospace, defence, transport, international aid and public-sector reform projects can combine this exposure with numerous technical and organisational dependencies. Structural complexity concerns those dependencies; temporal complexity concerns changing external conditions that may invalidate previously reasonable decisions.

The central challenge is to anticipate, survive or benefit from change while preserving the ability to act. Timing and positioning can become more important than optimising efficiency against the original plan. The outcome must be useful when delivered, even if it differs from the initial specification.

Typical symptoms include continually shifting requirements, work becoming irrelevant, uncertainty about the next change and reluctance to act until conditions settle. Managing these conditions requires active preparation rather than assuming that the original environment will return.

Where Ambiguity Comes From

A conceptual expression relates perceived complexity to three interacting features:

Perceived complexity ~ number of elements x interconnection x ambiguity

Here, ~ means a conceptual relationship rather than a calibrated numerical formula. Elements are the relevant components, interconnection concerns their relationships, and ambiguity concerns uncertainty in interpreting the situation. Without defined scales and units, the expression cannot produce a defensible numerical score.

Type

Main source of ambiguity

Structural

Monitoring and coordinating many dependencies

Technical

The solution space: how to achieve an outcome

Directional

The problem space: what should be achieved

Temporal

Constraints that can change during the project

A constraint is a condition limiting feasible action, such as regulation, available funding or an externally imposed approval requirement. Under temporal complexity, teams may need to prepare for several possible sets of constraints. Even initially clear objectives and methods may later change.

A subsystem is a component system within a larger system. Integrating information from subsystems becomes difficult when each is changing independently. Project elements are therefore usefully considered as options that may or may not remain relevant at delivery.

The Moving Fitness Landscape

A fitness landscape represents how well alternative approaches fit their environment. Peaks represent relatively favourable combinations; valleys represent less favourable ones.

When conditions are comparatively stable, a project can search for a better position on a relatively stable landscape. Under temporal complexity, the landscape resembles a rolling sea: favourable positions move, peaks become valleys and previously unattractive alternatives can become valuable.

A technically strong solution may fail if delivered at a politically or commercially unsuitable time. A less technically ambitious option may be more useful if it meets the current need when an opportunity opens. This does not make quality irrelevant; it changes how quality, relevance and timing must be considered together.

Options, Redundancy and Transition to Delivery

Keeping Options Available

A rigid project structure dedicated to a narrow capability can become obsolete as conditions change. Maintaining several developed alternatives spreads exposure across different possible futures.

Redundancy means deliberately retaining overlapping capability, knowledge or alternative solutions. It can support resilience when one option becomes unusable. Its cost must be recognised and justified rather than concealed.

Teams can explore alternatives separately and together, with frequent communication across boundaries. Involvement in more than one option can also reduce exclusive personal ownership of a single solution. Stakeholders may provide insights into environmental changes that the project team cannot see.

Phase Transitions

A phase transition is a substantial change in the project's mode of operation. A team may work gradually on several alternatives until a constraint becomes definite, disappears or is deferred. It can then stop parallel development and concentrate resources on rapid delivery of the selected option.

When structural and directional complexity are low, this transition may be relatively clear. Where structural, technical and directional complexity are also high, transitions may occur repeatedly and at unexpected times.

The aim is to deliver at an appropriate time, not merely to satisfy an obsolete date. However, externally determined opportunities also make detailed scheduling difficult.

Changing Constraints: An Abstract Example

Let A through H denote potential project elements. Let T(0) be the initial point, T(n) the later delivery point, and T(n-x) an intermediate point before delivery. These are time labels, not calculated dates.

T(0):      A B C D E F G H   Several constraints remain potential.
T(n-x):    A B C D E   G H   A realised constraint eliminates F.
T(n):      A B C D     G     Further constraints eliminate E and H.

Delivered combination: A + B + C + D + G

At the final point, constraints around B and C have dissipated, while constraints around A and D remain only potential. The plus signs mean combination of elements, not arithmetic addition. The example shows how the delivered configuration depends on which constraints actually materialise.

Management Approaches

Anticipation and Positioning

Planning combines:

• Anticipation: examining what might happen and where problems may arise.

• Positioning: preparing capabilities and options before the change occurs.

• Contingency planning: preparing responses to specified possible events.

• Planning by options: developing alternatives that fit different future conditions.

Options must be developed enough for rapid assessment and action. A list of undeveloped possibilities cannot provide the same readiness.

For large projects, mapping interconnected organisational or technical nodes can reveal weak points. Managers can examine whether local practices support the overall purpose and direct additional governance or resources toward vulnerable interfaces. A control-room approach builds a shared view of these dependencies while recognising that not all activity is visible or controllable.

Knowledge and Synchronisation

Project integration depends on timely knowledge transfer. Lead time is the interval needed before an activity or output becomes available; changes to it can disrupt dependent work.

Satisficing means reaching an acceptable outcome under the current conditions rather than proving a theoretical optimum. What counts as acceptable may change as knowledge and agreements change. A subsystem's local success is insufficient if its output arrives too late or does not fit the wider system.

Executive and Sponsor Support

Any phase may become critical if an external decision changes the direction or stops the work. Executives need to understand how established functional hierarchies affect integration and communication.

A meta-view is an overview of the whole project and its context rather than one technical component. Sponsors should provide this broader perspective continually, while trusting suitable managers with day-to-day delivery.

Important support includes:

• Explaining environmental changes and their implications directly.

• Defending justified redundancy and knowledge-transfer costs.

• Encouraging information exchange across subsystem boundaries.

• Formally closing obsolete plans before replacing them.

• Creating meaningful handovers and completion points so that repeated changes do not erase all sense of achievement.

Change weariness is fatigue and confusion arising from repeated alterations without sufficient explanation or closure.

Manager and Team Capabilities

Managers need flexibility across interfaces and alternatives, connections to unfamiliar communities of practice, and readiness to act when a suitable opportunity appears. A community of practice is a group sharing knowledge through a common field of work.

The burden should be shared across a connected management team rather than assigned to a single heroic individual. Managers also need to explain why an option has ended and help contributors release their investment in it.

Team continuity does not guarantee harmony: persistent relationships can also accumulate conflict. Behavioural differences can become increasingly important as people work together. Selection should consider working styles as well as expertise, and training should support knowledge sharing and coordination.

Finance, Scheduling, Risk and Procurement

Finance

Budgets need sufficient contingency reserves and explicit provision for maintaining alternatives and transferring knowledge. Estimates should recognise uncertainty rather than assume optimistic continuity. Public-sector funding cycles can create additional timing constraints.

Scheduling and Entrainment

Long front-end periods may be dominated by political approval and legitimacy rather than detailed construction tasks. In such periods, broad milestone targets may be more credible than tightly specified dates. A milestone is a significant decision or completion point, not a task duration.

Entrainment means synchronising activities with other important cycles or events. In project settings, these may include approvals, funding cycles, elections or the availability of dependent work. Synchronisation does not imply fixed, harmonious or perfectly predictable rhythms.

A pacer is an activity, role or mechanism that establishes the dominant timing rhythm around which other work is coordinated.

Risk

Important risks include externally imposed changes that are difficult to anticipate and the delivery of an unsuitable option at the wrong time.

• Unknown unknowns are relevant events or conditions that have not been recognised in advance.

• Black Swan describes a highly unexpected, consequential event; the term is not a precise probability estimate.

• Inadequate knowledge transfer between subsystems can cause rework, cost increases and delays.

Breaking risk into smaller tasks may obscure risks arising from the connections between tasks. Careful options analysis should assess each developed alternative so that a delivery decision can be made quickly when conditions permit. Otherwise the project may accumulate partially completed alternatives without delivering useful outcomes.

Procurement

Procurement is the process of obtaining goods, works or services. It must accommodate likely changes, avoid premature lock-in and allow timely deployment when a suitable option is approved.

• Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT): an arrangement combining construction, operation for a period and later transfer.

• Refurbish-Operate-Transfer (ROT): a similar arrangement involving refurbishment rather than initial construction.

Such arrangements can extend exposure from delivery into years of operation. Risk allocation depends on the actual contract rather than the label alone. Smaller procurement packages linked to manageable outputs may make change easier to handle and limit the scope of disputes. Lengthy approval processes or funding cycles can still prevent a timely response.

Mapping the Complexity

Mapping the Complexity is a structured discussion tool for identifying the kinds and levels of complexity a project faces. It helps decision-makers choose budgets, schedules, governance, resources and procurement approaches before interdependent risks become unmanageable.

A session can take approximately 60 minutes and use a whiteboard or large sheet of paper. Key decision-makers and relevant domain experts should participate. Repeat the analysis at the beginning of major phases and at control gates, which are formal points for reviewing progress and authorising the next stage.

Goals-and-Methods Matrix

The goals-and-methods matrix distinguishes uncertainty about ends from uncertainty about means.

2

The matrix helps distinguish technical uncertainty about methods from directional uncertainty about goals. These are illustrative patterns, not fixed classifications of every project in a sector. Declining clarity increases difficulty, but the matrix does not provide numerical failure probabilities.

The Base Map

Each row is rated from low to medium to high for a specified project phase.

Dimension

Focus

Structural

Number and significance of interdependencies

Technical

Impact of unresolved technology or design issues

Directional

Ambiguity and disagreement about goals

Temporal

Changing constraints and associated delays or timing dependence

Relational

Trust, openness, conflict, power differences, hidden agendas and informal networks

Relational analysis also considers stakeholder numbers, cross-organisational and cross-cultural communication, and whether informal networks support or weaken governance.

Dimension      Low -------- Medium -------- High
Structural     Position determined for the phase
Technical      Position determined for the phase
Directional    Position determined for the phase
Temporal       Position determined for the phase
Relational     Position determined for the phase

A mark represents a contextual judgement, not a universal complexity score.

Discussion Criteria

• Structural: scale; contractors, subcontractors and suppliers; present and future dependencies; pressure for tightly coordinated delivery.

• Technical: unresolved design issues; whether the team knows how to build the outcome; how time pressure restricts acceptable solutions.

• Directional: each participant's understanding of the objective; actual agreement; conflicting interests; time available for accommodation.

• Temporal: fixed start or operational dates; political and environmental dependencies; likely delays; monopoly suppliers that constrain alternatives.

• Relational: trust, information sharing, inclusion, conflict and differences in influence.

Seven Steps

Assemble decision-makers and relevant experts.

Draw the base map.

Explain the complexity dimensions.

Discuss each dimension and agree a current judgement of its level.

Mark the levels to create the map.

Repeat at major phase starts and significant decisions.

Use the resulting profile to adapt governance, responsibilities, contingency, resources and procurement.

Profiles should change as the project changes. Different forms of complexity may rise or fall at different times rather than moving together.

Cases

Information Technology Development

An information technology development project can have low directional complexity when its objective is agreed, medium-to-high structural complexity because of its scale, high technical complexity because it breaks new ground, and medium-to-high temporal complexity because rapid change in the surrounding technology forces design or scope revisions.

Appreciative Inquiry is a participatory approach that explores strengths and possibilities to develop a shared direction. Value Management is a structured process for clarifying required functions and assessing value. In this case, agreement about goals preceded agreement about solutions.

The initial account underestimated the problem because it relied on an incomplete analysis. Bringing stakeholders together exposed its actual nature and scale.

Hubble Space Telescope

Hubble received funding in the 1970s and was initially planned for launch in 1983. By early 1986, an October launch appeared feasible, but the Challenger disaster grounded the United States space shuttle fleet. Launch was delayed for several years.

During the delay, the telescope remained powered in a clean room with nitrogen purging, at an estimated storage cost of about US$6 million per month. Discovery launched it on 24 April 1990 on Space Transportation System mission 31, designated STS-31.

An initial estimate of approximately US$400 million grew to a construction cost above US$2.5 billion; estimated cumulative expenditure by 2010 was about US$10 billion. These figures refer to different cost scopes and periods, so they should not be treated as identical measures. The case illustrates how an external event can disrupt timing and add costs even when the project cannot control that event.

Large Engineering Projects

An examination of 60 large projects, including dams, urban infrastructure and oil platforms, identified front-end development periods averaging about seven years. Important risks included governments withdrawing commitments, slow or insufficient market development, challenges to legitimacy, macroeconomic shocks, political changes and partner restructuring.

The management implication is that lengthy development and institutional anchoring expose a project to new risks before physical delivery is complete.

Long Operating Horizons

Facilities associated with the 2000 Sydney Olympics illustrate why delivery cannot always be separated from later operation. Combining delivery with operating responsibilities can extend a short delivery focus into a five-to-ten-year horizon, increasing exposure to changing conditions.

Trevi Fountain

The Trevi Fountain in Rome illustrates continuity of a broad purpose alongside changing sponsors, designers and plans.

• In 1629, Pope Urban VIII asked Gian Lorenzo Bernini to develop possible improvements to an earlier fountain. That initiative was abandoned after the pope died, although some design ideas remained influential.

• Pope Clement XII organised a competition in 1730. Nicola Salvi received the commission after controversy over an initial result favouring Alessandro Galilei. Construction began in 1732.

• Salvi died in 1751 with the work incomplete. Giuseppe Pannini and sculptors including Pietro Bracci, Filippo della Valle, Giovanni Grossi and Andrea Bergondi contributed to its completion.

• The fountain was completed in 1762 and formally inaugurated by Pope Clement XIII on 22 May. The final design used allegorical figures rather than the originally planned statues of Agrippa and Trivia.

The project therefore experienced leadership changes, public controversy, designer succession and changes in the delivered design. The existence of alternative historical proposals does not establish that they were all maintained as active parallel project options.

Systems Mapping and Timeline Management

Mapping a System

A system is a set of interacting components whose relationships produce collective patterns of behaviour. A boundary identifies what is included in an analysis; a purpose or function identifies what the system does or is understood to achieve.

Systems mapping visualises interconnected parts to support understanding and intervention. A systemigram is a visual narrative showing connected entities and activities. It is related to, but not identical with, a map rating different types of project complexity.

A useful process is to:

Define the system and a manageable boundary.

Collect information, including directly from people who live or work within it.

Visualise relationships and examine feedback, missing connections, duplicated effort and misaligned incentives.

Validate interpretations with stakeholders.

Use the map to guide intervention and revisit it over time.

A feedback loop exists when a chain of effects returns to influence its starting condition. A leverage point is a place where intervention can have a substantial wider effect. A ripple effect is the spread of consequences through connected parts.

A map can be retrospective, comparing past configurations for evaluation, or prospective, exploring future intervention. In health-resource tracking in Namibia, mapping parallel approaches helped examine their integration and identify duplicated effort.

Conventional Timelines

A project timeline visualises tasks, duration and milestones. A Gantt chart is a time-scaled bar chart showing scheduled activity and, where represented, dependencies and progress. Timeline preparation involves identifying work, estimating durations, allocating resources and communicating the plan.

A sequential delivery model may move through planning, design, development, testing and deployment. Broader management activities include initiation, planning, execution, monitoring, control, closure and later review; these are not all necessarily separate sequential stages.

Conventional timelines remain useful for defined work, but temporal complexity weakens assumptions of stable constraints and predictable sequences. Milestones, developed alternatives and coordination with external cycles may then be more appropriate than treating a detailed initial schedule as permanently valid.
